newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Gonzalez denies state terrorism existed.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Gonzalez denies state terrorism existed.

text.p: Spain's former premier Felipe Gonzalez, whose 13-year government is being investigated about allegations it ran a "dirty war" against Basque separatists, said on Thursday his country was not guilty of state terrorism.

"Clearly, there hadn't been state terrorism in Spain," Gonzalez told a Spanish radio interviewer. "If there had been state terrorism, there wouldn't have been 900 victims from security forces, armed forces and civilians and 28...from supposed terrorists; the numbers would have been inverted."

Officials in Gonzalez's old Socialist administration, including a former interior minister, are on trial for their alleged part in setting up, funding and running death squads against ETA activists in the 1980s.

ETA, which means Basque Homeland and Freedom in the Basque language, has killed about hundreds of people since starting a campaign for Basque independence in 1968 and was killing about once a week when the dirty war was alleged to have started.
Ex-security chiefs and disgruntled Socialist leaders in the region have accused Gonzalez and his administration of organising the death squads, which murdered 27 alleged ETA members from 1983-87.

Gonzalez said "incidents" such as these had happened in many other democratic states when confronting "terrorist activity". "Incidents like those that have occurred in Spain, have happened in every country where terrorist activity has struck out at democracy," he added.
His comments provoked a fierce backlash from other political leaders.
Basque Nationalist Party spokesman Inaki Anasagasti angrily told journalists the statement that state terrorism never existed was "dangerous, unethical and bad for society".

"No one thinks that Felipe Gonzalez is going to say there was state terrorism," Anasagasti said. "The accusations we've made against him -- because we don't have proof against him personally -- are that he allowed the situation to exist and didn't stop it."
Gonzalez himself has eluded any court appearances in the scandal that forced an early election last March and helped put the conservative Popular Party (PP) in power.
The Supreme Court has yet to decide if the former premier will appear in court -- either as witness or suspect.
Some politicians believe Gonzalez carries no credibility anymore because of the pending court decision, due next month.

"He's just trying to deflect attention. State terrorism is as criminal as any other type, it can't be relegated to the second division," said Felipe Alcaraz, parliamentary spokesman for the United Left coalition.

The 54-year-old, whose charisma and youth once charmed a nation ready for change after nearly 40 years of the dictatorship of Francisco Franco, has visibly aged as the accusations pelted his Socialist Workers' Party.
But despite the difficulties, he told the radio interviewer he remained willing to lead.
"If the party asks me and God allows, I'll probably be the candidate in the next election," Gonzalez said.
